title: Team America: World Police
full_review:
The creators of "South Park" have turned from animation to puppetry in their latest big-screen extravaganza, which skewers everything from Broadway musicals to weapons of mass destruction. Inspired by the old British puppet animation series, "Thunderbirds," the film is an elaborate sendup of producer Jerry Bruckheimer's action films.

"Team America: World Police" (Paramount) from director Trey Parker -- in collaboration with his co-producer/creator/writing partner, Matt Stone -- concerns the exploits of an international police squad as it chases down terrorists across the world: Paris, Cairo, the Panama Canal and Korea.

The first we see of the team in action is a confrontation with Middle Eastern terrorists (the first of several wince-inducing racial stereotypes) in the famed City of Light, which by the time the shooting ends is totally decimated. Team leader Spottswoode later attends a Broadway play, "Lease" (read "Rent"), where star Gary Johnston is wowing them with a satiric song about AIDS (one of many bad-taste moments), and goes backstage afterward to speak with Gary.

After Spottswoode assures Gary that his interest in him is not sexual, but that he needs to help save the world by being a spy (in other words, to "act like a terrorist"), he brings Gary to the squad's elaborate headquarters -- housed behind the facade of Mount Rushmore -- where he introduces him to the team of Chris, the martial arts expert; Sarah, the clairvoyant; Lisa, the psychology expert; and Joe, the quarterback. Gary is told his help is needed to stop the terrorists or else devastation will be inevitable, and "all the worst parts of the Bible" will come true.

In spite of an immediate attraction to the blonde Lisa, Gary refuses the offer, until a soul-searching trip to Washington jogs his patriotism, and he decides duty to his country stands above all.

Cosmetically altered to look like a Middle Eastern terrorist, Gary and the team set out for Cairo, Egypt, where he becomes "Achmed" and narrowly escapes with his life.

Eventually he and the team take on Kim Jong Il, leader of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, who plans to destroy the world with WMD's, with the help of members of (uh-hem) F.A.G., the Film Actor's Guild, including such liberal Hollywood do-gooders as Alec Baldwin, Matt Damon, Michael Moore, Susan Sarandon, Sean Penn, Tim Robbins, Samuel L. Jackson and more. Baldwin comes in for special skewering.
The "real" people portrayed here are not immune to the puppet violence. To cite one example, the United Nations' Hans Blix is fed to a shark by Kim Jong Il, with graphically gruesome results.

There's a certain novelty in having puppets go through the motions of everything from kung fu moves to gross-out vomiting, but the sexual activity and the violence ultimately go way over the top.

The songs are not without wit, though sometimes -- as with the AIDS song -- are intentionally tasteless. A Ben Affleck putdown, "Pearl Harbor Sucked and I Miss You," and a paean to Alec Baldwin are funny in their loony way.

Everyone's fair game for spoofing in Stone and Parker's world: from the U.S. government -- sometimes accused of "policing the world," thus the "world police" concept -- to Hollywood's bleeding heart liberals. There's something to offend everyone, but the left gets it harder than the right. As indicated, bad taste abounds: even jokes about 9-11 -- the date, if not the actual events -- are included.

To give credit where it is due, the marionettes are quite amazing on a technical level (courtesy of the Chiodo brothers), but the level of sexual activity and gory violence -- albeit done in the name of humor -- makes the film impossible to endorse. They get points for the
production design which is eye-catching, witty and clever, to be sure.

Definitely not one for the kids, and probably not for most sensitive adults either.
Because of sexual activity both straight and gay, extreme violence, including dismemberment and blood, ethnic stereotypes, and crude and profane language, albeit all done by puppets, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
